paras: The lynching of Francisco Jimeno was the hanging of a young sheep-herder, described as Mexican or Indian, by about one hundred citizens near Lompoc, Santa Barbara County, California, in early April 1881. He had been arrested on suspicion of outraging and murdering Mrs. Louisa Sargent and was hanged after the inquest on her body. Papers across the country carried the story, and within days one dispatch reported that the wrong man had been lynched.

Mrs. Sargent, about twenty, the wife of John H. Sargent of Santa Rita near Lompoc, set out alone on horseback on a Saturday to visit a neighbor and did not return. Her husband found her horse grazing by the road, and the next morning searchers found her body buried near a sheep camp, her skull crushed. A sheep-herder from the camp was arrested, and the first dispatch reported "intense feeling" and a probability that he would be lynched.

Justice of the Peace A. Lansdell held an inquest, at which the herder, Francisco Jimeno, denied all knowledge and said he had been asleep under a tree. When the inquest ended, according to a Lompoc special to the Santa Barbara Press, one hundred citizens took him and hung him to a limb "for some seconds." Lowered, he said he had seen another man ravish and kill her and had dragged the body away and buried it to avoid suspicion; he then led the citizens to the club, her hat and her pail.

The citizens took his shoes fitting the tracks and his conflicting stories as proof of guilt and hanged him to a tree at or near the scene of the murder. The body was left hanging until the following afternoon, according to the Los Angeles Herald. An April 5 dispatch placed the hanging the previous night, while later reports said Tuesday or April 6.

Mrs. Sargent's funeral drew a very large attendance, with business houses closed. Parties then hunted Jimeno's brother, and a Lompoc special reported that he had been arrested and that the citizens would give him "a fair trial" and execute him if guilty. A Los Alamos special later said the brother proved an alibi through his employers, was released, and, frightened by "the vigilantes," fled to the brush. No report of an inquest on Jimeno or of any action against the lynchers appears in the coverage.

Most papers ran the Santa Barbara wire, which treated the herder as the murderer; the Chicago Tribune listed it in its "Criminal News" as a sheep-herder "Lynched at Santa Barbara." California papers endorsed the act: the Los Angeles Herald wrote that public sentiment in the county "fully justifies the hanging," and the Gold Hill Daily News reprinted the Santa Barbara Press's "All honor to Lompoc" and its call to do away with jury trials. The reports disagreed on who he was, calling him a Mexican, "a full-blooded Indian," or "Indian or Mexican."

The Wheeling Register took the opposite line, headlining "The Wrong Man Lynched" over a dispatch that blamed "a maddened mob of lynchers." Short notices naming him "Francisco Timino" circulated in Midwestern weeklies the following week.

Local dispatches called the evidence "very conclusive," but a San Francisco dispatch of April 7 said many citizens had protested Francisco's innocence and that evidence pointed to his older brother. The brother's release on an alibi left the question open, and accounts also differ on Jimeno's age, sixteen or eighteen.

bases: About one hundred citizens took an arrested sheep-herder after the inquest and hanged him to a tree (A7, A9, A6).

A crowd of about one hundred citizens hanged Jimeno without trial after a justice's inquest, on the ground that the evidence of murder and outrage was 'conclusive' (A7, A9, A4); the papers call it lynching and the act of 'Vigilantes' (A5, A16).
Separate Lompoc specials to the Santa Barbara Press (A7, A8), a San Luis Obispo dispatch (A9) and the wire (A4, A6) agree he was hanged; a later dispatch disputes his guilt, not the hanging (A19).

accounts.label: Lompoc specials to the Santa Barbara Press
accounts.gist: After the inquest one hundred citizens hanged Jimeno for some seconds; lowered, he said he had seen another man kill her and had dragged and buried the body; tracks, shoes and blood were taken as proof and he was hanged and left hanging.

accounts.label: Jimeno's statements, as reported
accounts.gist: He first said he was asleep under a tree; after the first hanging he said another man (in one version 'an unknown Mexican') did it and he hid the body to avoid suspicion.

accounts.label: San Francisco dispatch of April 7
accounts.gist: Many citizens had protested Francisco's innocence; evidence now showed his older brother was guilty, and citizens were hunting the brother with ropes.

accounts.label: Los Alamos special to the Santa Barbara Press
accounts.gist: The brother proved an alibi through his employers, was freed, and fled in fear of the vigilantes.

framing.detail: Los Angeles Herald: 'Public sentiment throughout the county fully justifies the hanging of the murderer.'
Gold Hill Daily News editorial 'Justice' mocked San Francisco juries and reprinted the Santa Barbara Press: 'All honor to Lompoc ... Away with the farce of jury trials.'
Chicago Tribune ran the wire under 'Lynched.' in its 'Criminal News' column, presenting the citizens' view that his guilt was 'beyond doubt'.
Wheeling Register headlined 'Mistaken Murderers. The Wrong Man Lynched by a California Crowd' and called the lynchers 'a maddened mob'.
